claims.claim: Eustathius was a native of Side in Pamphylia.
About 320 he was bishop of Beroea, and he became patriarch of Antioch shortly before the Council of Nicaea in 325.
Eustathius died c. 337, possibly in Thrace.
The work is titled Contra Ariomanitas et de anima, an anti-subordinationist treatise focusing on the soul.
The work debates whether the Word is immutable willfully or intrinsically, with Eustathius characterizing pro-Arian theology as arguing the former.
The work is now preserved in an epitome.
The work offers unprecedented opportunities for understanding Eustathius' theology, particularly his theological anthropology.
Eustathius was one of the most prominent opponents of Arianism at the Council of Nicaea and from 325-330 was engaged in an almost continuous literary warfare against the Arians.
Eustathius was deposed by a synod at Antioch in 330 for Sabellianism, which was confirmed by the emperor, and he was banished to Thrace.
Jerome mentions a De anima among Eustathius's works, and fragments are preserved of it.
